title: Food Science: The Chemistry and Physics of Cooking
department: Department of Food Science and Nutrition
description: A course for cooks who follow recipes with confidence and now want to know why they work. It explains cooking as chemistry and physics: how heat moves into food, what water, proteins, starches and fats do when they are heated, mixed and cooled, how browning makes flavor, how microbes ferment food or make it unsafe, and how we perceive flavor. Most sections come with a kitchen experiment that needs only ordinary equipment and a thermometer, and the companion book, Breakfast Cooking (CUL 101), puts the same science to work at the stove.
prerequisites: Comfortable following recipes and using basic kitchen equipment.
High-school chemistry helps (atoms, molecules, acids and bases); the essentials are reviewed where they are needed.
An instant-read digital food thermometer and a kitchen scale for the experiments.
objectives: Explain how heat reaches food by conduction, convection and radiation, and predict how pan, oven and water temperatures change cooking times.
Describe what heat, acid, salt and mixing do to proteins, starches and fats, and use that to diagnose a failed dish such as rubbery eggs, a lumpy sauce or a broken mayonnaise.
Distinguish the Maillard reaction, caramelization and enzymatic browning, and control browning with temperature, moisture and pH.
Explain how yeasts, bacteria and molds ferment foods, and why related microbes cause spoilage and illness.
Apply the USDA safe minimum internal temperatures, the danger zone and the 2-hour rule, and explain how each preservation method (cold, heat, drying, salt, sugar, acid) stops microbes.
Explain how taste, smell, texture and the trigeminal sense combine into flavor, and use that to season a dish.
Design, run and record a controlled kitchen experiment that changes one variable at a time.

chapters.title: Water and Heat
chapters.summary: Why water dominates cooking, what happens when it boils and evaporates, and the three ways heat moves into food.
chapters.challenge: Cook identical potato cubes in boiling water, in steam and in a 200°C (400°F) oven, time each until tender, and explain the order they finish in using heat transfer.

sections.title: The water molecule
sections.summary: Polarity and hydrogen bonds, and why water dissolves salt and sugar and holds so much heat.

sections.title: Boiling, simmering and evaporation
sections.summary: What a boiling point is, why it falls at high altitude, and why evaporation cools a wet surface and holds off browning.

sections.title: Conduction, convection and radiation
sections.summary: The three routes heat takes into food: from a hot pan, through moving water, oil or air, and from a glowing element or flame.

sections.title: Pans, ovens and thermometers
sections.summary: How the heat capacity and conductivity of cookware change cooking, why 100°C water cooks faster than 200°C oven air, and how to measure food temperature correctly.

chapters.title: Proteins
chapters.summary: How proteins unfold and bond together when they are heated, salted, acidified or beaten, shown in eggs, meat, fish, milk and wheat.
chapters.challenge: Using pasteurized eggs, cook eggs in water held at three different temperatures for the same time and match each texture to the egg proteins that have set.

sections.title: What a protein is
sections.summary: Chains of amino acids, how they fold, and the bonds that hold a protein in shape.

sections.title: Denaturation and coagulation
sections.summary: How heat, acid, salt and beating unfold proteins and let them link into a network, from set egg whites to cheese curds.

sections.title: Meat and fish: muscle and collagen
sections.summary: Why lean cuts toughen and dry out as they heat, while cuts rich in collagen turn tender with long, moist cooking.

sections.title: Gluten
sections.summary: How two wheat proteins form a stretchy network when flour meets water and is kneaded.

chapters.title: Carbohydrates and Starch
chapters.summary: Sugars, starches, pectins and gums: how they dissolve, crystallize, swell, thicken and go stale.
chapters.challenge: Thicken equal amounts of liquid with flour, cornstarch and potato starch, compare thickness, clarity and texture hot and again after a night in the refrigerator, and explain the results by gelatinization and retrogradation.

sections.title: Sugars
sections.summary: Glucose, fructose and sucrose: sweetness, solubility, crystals and how sugar holds on to water.

sections.title: Starch granules and gelatinization
sections.summary: Amylose and amylopectin, and how starch granules swell in hot water to thicken sauces and soften grains.

sections.title: Retrogradation and staling
sections.summary: Why bread goes stale faster in the refrigerator than on the counter, and why cooled starch gels firm up and weep.

sections.title: Pectin, gums and fiber
sections.summary: The cell-wall carbohydrates that set jam, thicken without starch and give vegetables their crunch.

chapters.title: Fats, Oils and Emulsions
chapters.summary: What fats are made of, how they behave in heat, and how emulsions such as mayonnaise and vinaigrette hold oil and water together.
chapters.challenge: Make mayonnaise with pasteurized egg yolk, break it on purpose by adding the oil too fast, rescue it, and explain each step with emulsion science.

sections.title: Triglycerides: saturated and unsaturated
sections.summary: How the shape of fatty acids explains why butter is solid and olive oil is liquid at room temperature.

sections.title: Fats in the heat
sections.summary: Frying, smoke points, and why oil breaks down when it is reused.

sections.title: Emulsions and emulsifiers
sections.summary: Droplets, lecithin and proteins, and why mayonnaise holds together while vinaigrette separates.

sections.title: Fat crystals: butter, pastry and chocolate
sections.summary: How the crystal forms of fat explain spreadable butter, flaky pastry and the snap of tempered chocolate.

chapters.title: Browning: Maillard and Caramelization
chapters.summary: The browning reactions that create the flavors of toast, seared meat and caramel, and how cooks control them.
chapters.challenge: Brown sliced onions three ways (dry pan, pan with a splash of water, and dry pan with a pinch of baking soda), then compare color, aroma, texture and time, and explain the differences.

sections.title: The Maillard reaction
sections.summary: How sugars and amino acids react under heat to make brown pigments and hundreds of aroma molecules.

sections.title: Caramelization
sections.summary: What happens when sugar is heated on its own, and how caramel differs from Maillard browning.

sections.title: Controlling browning: temperature, water and pH
sections.summary: Why a wet surface will not brown, why baking soda speeds browning, and how to get a good sear.

sections.title: Enzymatic browning
sections.summary: Why cut apples and avocados turn brown, and how acid, cold and blanching stop it.

chapters.title: Fermentation and Microbes
chapters.summary: How yeasts, bacteria and molds transform food, from bread, yogurt and sauerkraut to cheese and soy sauce, and why tested recipes keep fermentation safe.
chapters.challenge: Ferment a small batch of sauerkraut or yogurt following a tested recipe exactly, record its smell, sourness and appearance each day, and explain what the microbes are doing at each stage.

sections.title: Meet the microbes
sections.summary: Bacteria, yeasts and molds: what they eat, how fast they multiply, and what slows or stops them.

sections.title: Yeast fermentation: bread, beer and wine
sections.summary: How yeast turns sugar into carbon dioxide and alcohol, and what that does to dough and drinks.

sections.title: Lactic acid fermentation
sections.summary: How lactic acid bacteria sour yogurt, sauerkraut, kimchi and sourdough, and why the acid protects the food.

sections.title: Molds and koji
sections.summary: The molds that ripen cheese and make soy sauce and miso, and how they differ from the molds that spoil food.

chapters.title: Food Safety and Preservation
chapters.summary: What makes food unsafe and the science behind every preservation method, built on the USDA rules: keep food out of the 40 to 140°F (4 to 60°C) danger zone, refrigerate within 2 hours (1 hour above 90°F, 32°C), and cook to safe minimum internal temperatures checked with a thermometer.
chapters.challenge: Audit your own kitchen: check that the refrigerator holds 40°F (4°C) or below and the freezer 0°F (-18°C) or below, check your thermometer in ice water, and write a safety plan for one meal using the USDA safe minimum internal temperatures.

sections.title: Pathogens and how they make us sick
sections.summary: The main bacteria, viruses and toxins behind foodborne illness, and why spores and some toxins survive cooking.

sections.title: Time, temperature and the danger zone
sections.summary: Why bacteria multiply fastest between 40 and 140°F (4 and 60°C), the 2-hour rule (1 hour above 90°F, 32°C), and refrigerator and freezer temperatures.

sections.title: Cooking to safe temperatures
sections.summary: The USDA safe minimum internal temperatures: 145°F (63°C) with a 3-minute rest for whole cuts of beef, pork, veal and lamb, 160°F (71°C) for ground meats and egg dishes, and 165°F (74°C) for poultry and leftovers.

sections.title: Preservation: cold, heat, drying, salt, sugar and acid
sections.summary: How each method stops or slows microbes, explained by temperature, water activity and pH.

chapters.title: Flavor Perception
chapters.summary: How taste, smell, touch and the chemical sense combine in the brain into flavor, and how cooks use that knowledge to season.
chapters.challenge: Run a blind tasting: identify foods with your nose open and pinched shut, then test how a pinch of salt changes the bitterness of grapefruit or strong coffee, and explain both results.

sections.title: Taste: the five basic tastes
sections.summary: Sweet, sour, salty, bitter and umami, their receptors, and why the tongue map is a myth.

sections.title: Smell and retronasal aroma
sections.summary: Why most of what we call flavor is smell, sensed from the back of the mouth as we chew and swallow.

sections.title: Texture, temperature and the chemical sense
sections.summary: Mouthfeel, and the trigeminal nerve that feels the burn of chili and the cool of mint.

sections.title: Balancing flavor
sections.summary: How salt, acid, sweetness, bitterness and fat change each other, and why people taste the same food differently.

preface:
This book is for cooks who can already follow a recipe and now want to know why it works. Why does a steak brown in a hot, dry pan and turn gray in a crowded one? Why does mayonnaise hold together, and why does it sometimes break? Why does bread go stale faster in the refrigerator than on the counter? Each of these questions has an answer in chemistry or physics, and the answers make you a better cook, because once you know what is happening in the pan you can fix what goes wrong.

We start with water and heat, since nearly all cooking is water being heated. Then we take the main molecules of food one at a time (proteins, carbohydrates and fats), watch what heat does to each, and see how they combine when food browns. The last three chapters turn to living things and to ourselves: the microbes that ferment food or spoil it, the rules that keep food safe, and the senses that turn chemistry into flavor.

Three foods run through the whole book: an egg, a loaf of bread and a seared steak. Between them they show nearly every reaction in these pages. Most sections end with a kitchen experiment that needs nothing more than a pan, a scale and a good thermometer. Change one thing at a time, write down what you see, and you are doing food science.

This book has a practical companion, Breakfast Cooking, which takes these ideas to the stove one morning at a time. Read them in either order; each points to the other.

bible.teacher: Dr. Professor teaches this book as a food scientist who cooks: every technique is explained by the molecules and microbes involved, and every explanation is tested with a kitchen experiment. Mechanisms come from McGee and the food science textbooks, practical tests from López-Alt, and every safety rule from USDA FSIS, quoted exactly.
bible.promise: By the last page you will look at any recipe and say what each step does to the food, predict what will happen if you change it, and keep the food safe while you experiment.
threads: Food is mostly water, and cooking is mostly moving heat into it: every chapter comes back to water and temperature.
Structure explains behavior: proteins, starches and fats act as they do because of their shapes and bonds.
One variable at a time: each chapter has an experiment with a control, a single change and a written record.
Safety is science too: USDA temperatures and times are stated exactly, with the microbiology that explains them.
From theory to the stove: chapters point to the matching cook-along in the companion book, Breakfast Cooking (CUL 101).

runningExamples.name: The egg
runningExamples.use: Proteins in their purest kitchen form: heat transfer into the shell (Ch 1), coagulation of white and yolk (Ch 2), yolk lecithin in mayonnaise (Ch 4), browned edges of a fried egg (Ch 5), Salmonella and the 160°F (71°C) rule for egg dishes (Ch 7).

runningExamples.name: A loaf of bread
runningExamples.use: Gluten (Ch 2), starch gelatinization and staling (Ch 3), crust browning (Ch 5), yeast and sourdough fermentation (Ch 6), mold spoilage (Ch 7) and the aroma of fresh bread (Ch 8).

runningExamples.name: A seared steak
runningExamples.use: Conduction and choice of pan (Ch 1), muscle proteins and collagen (Ch 2), rendered fat (Ch 4), the Maillard crust (Ch 5), and 145°F (63°C) with a 3-minute rest (Ch 7).

runningExamples.name: The kitchen notebook
runningExamples.use: The reader's record of every experiment: the question, the one variable changed, what was held constant, the result and the explanation.

conventions: Give every temperature in both °C and °F; quote USDA safety temperatures exactly as USDA states them, in °F, with the Celsius conversion in parentheses (145°F, 63°C).
Name a molecule plainly first, then technically ("the main egg-white protein, ovalbumin").
Say which explanations are well established and which are still debated by food scientists.
Never round, relax or offer shortcuts on a safety number; temperatures and times come only from current USDA FSIS guidance.
Refer back to earlier chapters by number, and to the companion book by chapter title ("see Breakfast Cooking, Chapter 1, Eggs Every Way").

bible.care: Food safety is taught as fixed rules with the science behind them, never as a matter of taste. State plainly where they apply: keep perishable food out of the danger zone, 40 to 140°F (4 to 60°C); refrigerate within 2 hours, or 1 hour when it is above 90°F (32°C); keep the refrigerator at 40°F (4°C) or below and the freezer at 0°F (-18°C) or below; and cook to the USDA safe minimum internal temperatures, checked with a food thermometer: 145°F (63°C) with a 3-minute rest for whole cuts of beef, pork, veal and lamb, 160°F (71°C) for ground meats and egg dishes, and 165°F (74°C) for all poultry and for leftovers. Any experiment that uses raw or lightly cooked egg calls for pasteurized eggs, which USDA says may be used without cooking. Fermentation experiments follow a tested recipe exactly, and when in doubt, throw it out. Low-temperature cooking and home canning are explained as science (why time matters as well as temperature, why low-acid foods carry a botulism risk) but not taught as procedures; readers who want to try them are sent to current, tested USDA instructions.
